title: Superconducting singlet-triplet qubits
authors: Anatoliy Lotkov, Maria Spethmann, Daniel Loss
abstract: Hybrid devices integrating quantum dots with Josephson junctions are gaining interest because they combine spin-based quantum computing with circuit quantum electrodynamics (circuit QED) methods. In particular, Andreev spin qubits have shown significant experimental progress including strong two-qubit coupling, and are predicted to exhibit all-to-all connectivity. Here we propose superconducting singlet-triplet (SST) qubits that rely on parallel-aligned double quantum dots in Josephson junctions. While Andreev spin qubits require spin-orbit interaction to unlock the spin degree-of-freedom, SST qubits do not require spin-orbit interaction, making the advantages of hybrid devices available to a wider range of materials. Similar to Andreev spin qubits, the qubit states couple to the superconducting phase across the junction, which allows for control and readout using circuit QED, and supports all-to-all connectivity. Only $N$ flux lines are required to perform any single- and two-qubit gate among $N$ qubits, and thus the overhead of control lines is small. Finally, linear protection from charge or flux noise makes these qubits interesting candidates for a future quantum processor.
summary: This paper introduces and theoretically analyzes Superconducting Singlet-Triplet (SST) qubits, which are promising candidates for scalable quantum processors because they avoid the need for spin-orbit coupling. The authors derive the effective Hamiltonian by treating the system in the transmon regime and utilize advanced perturbation theory to map out robust control protocols for single and two-qubit gates.
main_problem: The paper proposes superconducting singlet-triplet (SST) qubits as a robust alternative to Andreev spin qubits for quantum computation.
main_result: These SST qubits maintain the advantages of coupling to circuit QED while crucially eliminating the need for spin-orbit interaction, making them compatible with a wider range of materials like silicon.
method: The effective qubit Hamiltonian is derived using Schrieffer-Wolff transformations and by analyzing the system in the transmon regime. Control mechanisms are mapped out based on manipulating superconducting phases ($\phi_j$).
model_or_system: The physical platform consists of parallel-aligned double quantum dots integrated into Josephson junctions, forming an array of $N$ qubits coupled to a superconducting circuit. The Hamiltonian incorporates terms for charging energy ($E_C$), Josephson coupling ($E_J$), and crossed Andreev couplings ($E_{CA}$).
key_observables: Dispersive shift ($\chi_n(s)$) and Lamb shift ($\Lambda_n(s)$) are key observables used to characterize qubit-cavity coupling for readout.
important_parameters: The analysis relies on regimes where $\Gamma, |\delta h| \ll |\epsilon| \ll U, \Delta$, and specifically assumes the transmon regime ($E_c \ll E_J$) for effective Hamiltonian derivation.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include operating in the dispersive regime for readout ($\omega_r - \omega_{tr} \gg g$), treating Zeeman coupling as a small perturbation, and neglecting higher-order terms during the Schrieffer-Wolff expansion.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the single SST qubit structure, while Figure 2 shows the array setup for $N$ qubits. The text references Hamiltonian equations (Eqs. 3, 4, 5) and cavity coupling details (Eqs. 7, 8).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and proposing SST qubits over Andreev qubits, to deriving the full system Hamiltonian, simplifying it via Schrieffer-Wolff transformations in the transmon regime, and finally detailing control schemes for single-qubit gates (X/Z set points) and two-qubit entangling gates.
why_interesting: The detailed derivation of an effective Hamiltonian from a complex superconducting circuit model using advanced many-body techniques like Schrieffer-Wolff is highly relevant to understanding controllable quantum hardware architectures in condensed matter physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A superconducting singlet-triplet qubit consisting of a double quantum dot in a Josephson junction. The spins in the quantum dots are coupled by crossed Andreev processes across the junction, ECA(1 + cos ϕ), whose magnitude can be controlled by the superconducting phase ϕ. Additionally, a difference in the dots’ Zeeman energies δh mixes singlet and triplet states.

Figure 2. To operate N SST qubits, they are placed in par- allel in a superconducting circuit where they are controlled by magnetic fluxes Φj, analogous to a setup suggested for Andreev spin qubits [13]. A conventional Josephson junction with large Josephson energy EJ enables two-qubit interac- tions.

Figure 3. Superconducting singlet-triplet (SST) qubits are operated by changing the fluxes through the adjacent circuit loops, which change the superconducting phases across them (black arrows). Qubits in their OFF flux set points are in an idle state. Qubits in their X flux set point are subject to single-qubit rotations. Single-qubit rotations can be performed for different qubits at once. Any two qubits that are in their INT flux set point interact and can realize a two-qubit gate.

Figure 4. The S12 coefficient [Eq. (10)] of the scattered waveg- uide photons as a function of the magnetic flux φs j. The S12 coefficient is plotted for two possible states of the jth qubit sj = ±1. The other magnetic fluxes are tuned to the INT set point (φs k̸=j = π/2) to make the respective qubits not affect the photon scattering phase. The plot clearly shows that the maximum difference between the scattering phases for the qubit states sj = ±1 is achieved in the OFF set point (φs j = π) and the X set point (φs j = 0). The S12 coefficient is plotted for the following parameter values: κ/h = 20 MHz, ωp/2π = ωr/2π = 4 GHz, EJ/h = 45 GHz, EC/h = 100 MHz, ECA/h = 2 GHz, g/h = 100 MHz.
